title: The browser frontend and the two non-Rust test suites

overview.l1: This is the part of Bible Atlas that runs in your browser, plus everything that tests it without touching Rust. Five small JavaScript files draw the /world map -- tiles, glowing place markers, narrative arrows, and historical borders that reshape as you drag the time slider -- and handle a few reader-page tricks (scrolling to a verse, keeping buttons pinned) only real browser code can do; everything else is C#. Two test suites check this from the outside: 54 Playwright browser tests plus math law tests, and 39 xunit tests checking C# logic in isolation, no browser needed. This is also the part of the app its owner plans to eventually replace, so every file explains what it draws and which server data feeds it.
overview.l2: The JS layer (client/wwwroot/js/) is five ES modules with no build step: geo.js is pure sphere math (lat/lon <-> unit vector, spherical interpolation); border-morph.js is the pure lookup/overlay/animate combinator deciding which curated border shapes apply to a time window and how to blend between them; map.js is the one large file (4,049 lines) that owns the actual Leaflet map instance, its markers/labels/clusters/hover-arbitration, and two custom layer classes (ArrowLayer, BorderLayer) that paint narrative arrows and polity borders as SVG; reader.js and lazyProse.js are grab-bags of DOM-measurement/scroll/observer helpers the reader page and its popovers call via Blazor's JS interop, since C# alone can't ask the real rendered page a geometry question. tests/ux/ is a Playwright + fast-check TypeScript suite that couples ONLY to CONTRACT.md's data-testid inventory plus the raw HTTP API -- never to Blazor internals -- organized around world/map behavior, the reader and its whole-Bible passage coverage, the popover/frontier content platform, pure-HTTP API properties, the state-atom migration's visible behavior, and cross-cutting app features. fast-check is a property-testing library: instead of one hand-picked example, a property test generates hundreds of random-but-valid inputs (e.g. "some real verse") and checks a rule holds for all of them; the FC_NUM_RUNS environment variable controls how many. client.Tests/ and client.ContractTests/ are separate C# xunit projects testing pure logic classes directly (no bUnit, no live server) plus a Reqnroll/Gherkin harness proving the client's own DTOs satisfy the same atlas-query-contract feature files a Rust cucumber harness binds independently.
overview.l3: Notable cross-cutting facts: map.js exposes a family of `debug*` exports (never called from production Blazor code) purely so Playwright tests can reach its live module state -- real camera/zoom, land-mask geometry, mid-morph path data -- via a dynamic `import('/js/map.js')` inside `page.evaluate`, rather than re-deriving the same math a second time in a test. border-morph.js and geo.js are framework-agnostic and importable from plain Node, which is how tests/ux/geo.spec.ts proves ~10 geometric laws (round-trip identity, unit-vector closure, slerp identities, rotation isometry) against 3,000 fast-check-generated cases with zero browser cost. The UX suite's own lib/ directory (8 files) holds shared oracles -- black-box reimplementations of client-side logic (hovercard.ts mirrors PlaceCard.razor's verse-reveal rule; years.ts mirrors YearText.cs) -- deliberately kept independent of the client so a bug shared by both copies is unlikely. Several conformance-style xunit files (AsyncMemoConformanceTests, PopoverChromeConformanceTests, FrontierMatrixConformanceTests, State/ConformanceTests, State/ViewRegistryConformanceTests) share one discipline: scan the real client/ source tree with a bounded regex, then prove the scan has real teeth by running it against a deliberately planted violation too -- never trusting a check that has only ever seen a clean tree. client.Tests carries NO bUnit reference (confirmed via its own .csproj) -- disclosed explicitly in ViewStateServiceTests.cs's own header: this project tests pure logic/static classes only; actual Razor-component rendering is exercised exclusively by the Playwright suite. The AQC (atlas query contract) fixtures are committed JSON files under contracts/atlas-query-contract/fixtures/, replayed by client.ContractTests/Steps/AqcSteps.cs against the SAME .feature files (linked in, not copied) a separate Rust harness binds -- CorpusCountTests.cs enforces, by reflection, that both sides execute the identical scenario count.

files.role: Pure sphere math: lat/lon <-> unit vector, slerp, ring resampling.
files.l1: This file is the ruler and compass for the map's globe. Everywhere else in the app talks in latitude/longitude, like an address; this file's own private language is a point on a ball, a "unit vector". It converts between the two, and it knows how to walk smoothly along the surface of that ball from one point to another (slerp), which is what makes a kingdom's border morph smoothly from its old shape to its new one as you drag the time slider. If this file vanished, borders could still be drawn but could never smoothly animate between two eras -- they would only ever jump.
files.l2: geo.js is a small, framework-agnostic ES module -- no Leaflet, no DOM -- so it can be imported both by the browser (map.js/border-morph.js) and directly by a plain Node test (tests/ux/geo.spec.ts), with zero browser needed for the math itself. Its core pair is `toVec(phi, lambda)`/`fromVec(v)`, converting radian latitude/longitude to/from a 3D unit vector `[x, y, z]`; `toVecDeg`/`fromVecDeg` are thin degree-based wrappers over that pure core, matching this app's own [lat, lon]-in-degrees convention. `slerp(a, b, t)` (spherical linear interpolation) walks smoothly between two unit vectors, falling back to a plain lerp+normalize when the two points are numerically identical (dividing by near-zero would blow up). `resampleRing`/`buildCorrespondence`/`slerpRing` turn two differently-shaped curated border rings into two arrays of the SAME point count, index-paired so each point in the old ring has a matching point in the new one to slide toward. Every function is a plain array-in, array-out function -- no classes, no shared state -- which is what makes it trivial to test standalone.
files.l3: `toVec`/`fromVec` (geo.js:53,87) are the proven forward/inverse maps; `fromVec` deliberately uses `atan2(z, hypot(x,y))` rather than `asin(z)` for latitude, because asin's derivative diverges near the poles and would amplify float error -- see the doc comment's own two-line unit-norm proof. `slerp` (geo.js:177) implements the standard sin-weighted formula and re-normalizes its output unconditionally, because the raw weighted sum can drift measurably off unit length exactly where sin(theta) is ill-conditioned (near theta=0 or pi) -- a real property-test-shrunk case is cited in the comment. `resampleRing` (geo.js:257) walks a ring's arc length with a single forward-only two-pointer scan (O(n+m), not O(n*m)) to place n evenly-spaced points; `buildCorrespondence` (geo.js:374) additionally normalizes winding direction (`windingSign`) and picks a start-vertex offset (`bestStartOffset`, brute-force O(n^2), a one-time per-era-pair cost) so slerped pairs don't produce a twisted, self-crossing morph. Every law here (round-trip identity, unit-vector closure, slerp endpoint/symmetry/planarity identities, rotation as an orthogonal transform, resampleRing's point-0-on-source-vertex guarantee) is proven by thousands of fast-check-generated inputs in tests/ux/geo.spec.ts, not merely asserted in comments -- "the laws are the tests". Known, disclosed gap: `fromVec`'s round-trip law only holds strictly inside the open interval (-90deg, 90deg) -- longitude is genuinely unrecoverable exactly at a pole, which this app's curated data never places a vertex on. Called by border-morph.js's `lookup`/`animate` combinators; never touches Leaflet or the DOM.

files.role: The lookup/overlay/animate combinator that resolves a polity's era geometry for any time window.
files.l1: When you drag the time slider, a kingdom's border on the map has to do one of two things: sit still showing all its historical shapes layered together, or smoothly reshape itself as you scrub through time. This file is the one place that decides, for any polity and any time window, which curated border shapes are relevant (`lookup`), how to style them when several eras are shown at once (`overlay`), and how to blend between two eras mid-drag (`animate`). map.js's BorderLayer is the only thing that paints pixels; this file only ever decides shapes and styling. If it vanished, the map could still show borders for a fixed year, but dragging the slider across an era boundary would only ever jump, never morph.
files.l2: This is a small, pure ES module (no Leaflet, no DOM) built directly on geo.js's slerp/correspondence math. `lookup(roster, from, to)` filters the full flat polity-era roster down to whichever eras intersect the given window, grouped by polity id into a `Map`, sorted oldest to newest -- deliberately mirroring the Rust server's own filter (`TimeRange::intersects`, "by id then from") as a second, parallel implementation, since a browser drag frame can't afford a network round trip. `overlay(lines)` is pure styling: it tags each era "oldest"/"middle"/"newest" for CSS's dotted-to-solid style ramp, without touching geometry. `animate(lines, atYear)` is the scrub path: for a single visible era it's the identity (no morph needed); for two or more, it piecewise-slerps between whichever pair of eras bracket `atYear`, using a small in-memory cache (`correspondenceCache`, a `Map`) so each adjacent-era-pair's correspondence is computed once and reused across every drag frame. A ring-count mismatch between adjacent eras (a rare topology change) snaps rather than fabricating an in-between shape.
files.l3: `lookup` (border-morph.js:58) groups by `entry.id` and sorts by `from`; `overlay` (border-morph.js:90) augments each entry with `age`/`tierIndex`/`tierCount` only. `animate` (border-morph.js:166) computes each era's "knot" as the midpoint of its own [from,to] span (`knotYear`, line 137) -- deliberately not the raw boundary years, since adjacent curated eras touch at adjacent years and using raw edges would squeeze the whole morph into one simulated year. `cachedCorrespondence` (line 111) keys the cache as `"{id}:{fromA}-{fromB}:{ringIndex}"` and calls `geo.js`'s `buildCorrespondence` with n=128 on first use; `clearCorrespondenceCache` is a test-only reset. A polity whose adjacent eras carry a different number of disjoint rings (e.g. Ptolemaic Egypt's Nile+Cyrenaica pair vs. an earlier single-ring era) has no well-defined per-vertex correspondence, so that ring snaps to whichever era is nearer in local t rather than inventing a topology-changing in-between shape -- disclosed in the doc comment, not silently smoothed. map.js's BorderLayer is the sole consumer: it calls `lookup` once per window/roster change or per drag frame, then either `overlay` (settled display) or `animate` (mid-drag), and paints whatever ring coordinates come back -- "no separate data paths, no pair-shaped special case" is literally true of this module's shape. No dedicated unit-test file imports this module directly (unlike geo.js); its behavior is exercised end-to-end through map.js's `debug*` exports by tests/ux/world-border-morph.spec.ts, while the underlying slerp/correspondence math it calls into is separately proven by tests/ux/geo.spec.ts.

files.role: IntersectionObserver-based lazy fetch trigger for Kretzmann commentary prose.
files.l1: The Kretzmann commentary page could try to fetch every paragraph's text the instant you open a chapter, but for a long chapter that means dozens of requests firing at once for text you haven't scrolled to yet. This tiny file instead watches each commentary row and tells the C# side to fetch that one row's text only once it's about to scroll into view. If it vanished, the page would fall back to fetching everything up front the moment the chapter loads -- correct, just wasteful.
files.l2: Two exported functions, `observeProseItems(dotnetRef, selector)` and `unobserveProseItems()`, wrap a single module-scoped `IntersectionObserver`. `observeProseItems` first tears down any prior observer, then (if `IntersectionObserver` exists in this environment) watches every element matching `selector` with a generous `rootMargin: '800px'` so a fetch starts well before the row is actually visible; each row is `unobserve`d the moment it intersects (a one-shot trigger -- the real "already requested" guard lives on the C# side). If `IntersectionObserver` isn't available at all, it degrades to requesting every item immediately, rather than leaving prose permanently unfetched -- "fail toward correctness, not silence", the same philosophy this app applies to every other optional browser capability. `dotnetRef.invokeMethodAsync` is the JS-to-.NET call: Blazor's interop bridge, letting this plain JS callback drive a C# method.
files.l3: `_observer` (lazyProse.js:24) is module-scoped, not returned to the caller, since exactly one Kretzmann.razor instance is ever mounted at a time. `observeProseItems` (line 26) reads `entry.target.dataset.kretzmannItemId` and calls back `OnItemNearViewport` on `dotnetRef`; Kretzmann.razor's own `SemaphoreSlim(8)` gate (not in this file) separately bounds ACTUAL concurrent fetches -- this module only ever decides WHEN a fetch is requested, never how many run at once. This module is the disclosed client-side mitigation for KRETZ-PROSE-SCALE: the real fix (widening the chapter-scoped listing response to carry prose inline, collapsing back to one request) is a parked, future server change; this file exists because the batch's own standing rule was zero server changes. Called from client/Pages/Kretzmann.razor only.

files.role: DOM-measurement and scroll/geometry interop helpers for the Bible reader and its popovers.
files.l1: This file is the reader page's toolbox for anything that needs to ask the real, rendered browser page a question C# can't answer on its own: "where is this verse right now?", "has the user scrolled?", "how tall is the header, exactly?", "is my mouse still over this popover?". It scrolls a clicked verse into view, remembers your scroll position so it survives navigating away and back, keeps the fixed prev/next chapter buttons pinned at the right height as you scroll, and works out where a popover can safely open without spilling off-screen. If it vanished, the reader would still render text, but verse links wouldn't jump to the right place, scroll position would reset on every navigation, and popovers could render cut off or in the wrong spot.
files.l2: reader.js is a flat collection of exported functions, each independently callable from Blazor via JS interop (`IJSObjectReference`) -- there is no shared object or class, just plain module-scoped `let` variables holding whichever single cleanup callback is currently active (e.g. `_scrollCleanup`, `_navCenterCleanup`), following a consistent "replace any prior listener, then return a matching `unwatch*` to tear it down" pattern. Several functions (`findReaderScrollContainer`/`findScrollContainer`) walk up the DOM from a `data-testid` root reading `getComputedStyle(node).overflowY`, to find whichever ancestor is the REAL scrolling container right now -- standalone (the whole document scrolls) versus split view (a pane scrolls internally) are genuinely different layouts, and this walk is what lets one function (`setScrollY`/`watchScroll`) work correctly in both without being told which mode it's in. `watchChapterNavCenter` recomputes a CSS custom property (`--chapter-nav-top`) synchronously on every scroll event -- not `requestAnimationFrame`-throttled like `watchScroll` -- because a one-frame lag there is visible as the fixed nav buttons briefly "teleporting", confirmed by a root-cause trace, not a guess. `getPaneRect`/`getVerseAnchorRect`/`getElementRect` each return a viewport-relative rectangle a popover component uses to clamp or center itself; `isPointInsideEither` and `capturePointer` support pointer-tracking edge cases (a peek staying open, a split divider drag) that Blazor's own event model can't express directly.
files.l3: Notable exports: `scrollToVerse(n)`/`scrollFocalRowIntoView(domId)` (reader.js:7,30) implement the `#v{n}` anchor contract (CONTRACT.md); `watchShiftRelease`/`unwatchShiftRelease` (line 60) listen on `window.blur`/`document.visibilitychange` to reset a stuck shift-held flag when focus leaves the tab mid-keypress -- Blazor has no binding for either event. `findScrollContainer`/`findReaderScrollContainer` (lines 109, 121) are the single "which element really scrolls" decision, re-derived from a live computed style every call rather than a hardcoded class name, so it survives future CSS restructuring; `scrollToTop`, `setScrollY`, `watchScroll` all build on it. `watchChapterNavCenter` (line 414) is the most heavily-revised function in the file -- three documented fix rounds (HOTFIX-3, then a further NAV-STUTTER-2 root-cause) chase a one-frame position lag caused by `requestAnimationFrame` deferral and, later, by an inherent compositor-vs-main-thread event ordering; the final fix skips binding a listener at all when standalone (no scroll container found), since with `contain: layout` scoped only to split mode, a pure-CSS `50vh` fallback is then correct with zero JS involved. `getElementRect`/`isPointInsideEither` (lines 573, 619) are the only two functions here explicitly keyed off a real `ElementReference` rather than a CSS selector, because ArrowNav can mount up to four simultaneous instances with no unique class to select by. `capturePointer` (line 649) calls the native `setPointerCapture`, which Blazor's `PointerEventArgs` has no binding for at all. Called from client/Components/SplitDivider.razor, MiniReaderExpand.razor, ArrowNav.razor, ExplorerPopover.razor, and client/Pages/Reader.razor, Concord.razor, CompositionSplit.razor -- reader.js's functions are reused wherever a second reading surface (Concord) needs the identical real-scroll-container logic.

files.role: The Leaflet world map: tiles, markers, labels, narrative arrows, polity borders, and era morphing.
files.l1: This one file draws everything you see on the /world map: the tan relief basemap, the glowing "ember" markers for lit-up places and the small quiet dots for the rest of the graph, their name labels, curated landmark labels, the colored narrative arrows connecting places in a story, and the historical kingdom borders that reshape as you drag the time slider. It also decides which marker your mouse actually meant when several sit close together, when to collapse a crowd of markers into one cluster glyph, and when a label must hide to avoid colliding with another. Everything it draws is fed to it by C# (MapInterop.cs), which has already fetched the data from the server. If this file vanished, /world would have no map at all; every other page would still work.
files.l2: map.js is one ES module shared by every Leaflet map instance on the page (the full map and any number of popover mini-maps), keyed by a small integer id in a module-level `instances` Map -- `init()` returns an id, and every other export takes that id first. It's organized around a few concerns: (1) marker lifecycle -- `setScene` diffs an incoming place list against existing Leaflet markers by id, so a refresh never tears down a marker mid-hover; (2) anti-collision -- `applyMarkerNudges` displaces near-coincident markers by a bounded number of SCREEN pixels (never a fixed geographic distance), and `applyMarkerClusters` collapses a dense pileup into one numbered glyph at wide zoom; (3) hover/click arbitration -- `resolveHoverTarget` picks the true nearest candidate by real screen distance, never trusting whichever DOM element the browser's own z-order routed the event to; (4) label declutter -- `applyLabelTier` grid-buckets every label and lets only the highest-priority one per cell survive, re-run every zoom; (5) two custom Leaflet layer classes, `ArrowLayer` (narrative arrows as bezier SVG paths) and `BorderLayer` (per-polity era border rings as three stacked SVG paths, plus the era-morphing state machine driven by border-morph.js). A family of `debug*` exports (never called from production C#) lets Playwright tests reach this module's live state via a dynamic `import('/js/map.js')`, reading the real camera/zoom/geometry directly rather than reimplementing map.js's own math inside a test.
files.l3: `init` (map.js:103) creates one `L.map` locked to `BIBLICAL_WORLD_BOUNDS`, adds the tile layer (Esri World_Shaded_Relief, Carto fallback on `tileerror`), and -- non-mini only -- creates four dedicated panes so paint order is independent of DOM insertion order, then constructs `BorderLayer`/`ArrowLayer`. `setScene` (line 404) diffs `scene.places`/`quiet_places` against live markers, then runs `applyMarkerClusters` -> `applyMarkerNudges` -> `buildLitByName` -> `applyLabelTier` -> `ArrowLayer.setArrows` in fixed order. `resolveHoverTarget` (line 1083) finds every candidate within `HIT_RADIUS_PX` (26px, the marker hit-circle diameter), returns the nearest, and opens a chooser flyout when 2+ true positions are genuinely coincident within `AMBIGUITY_RADIUS_PX` (3px); `isTrustedPointerEvent` (line 1172) skips arbitration for a script-dispatched event, since a synthetic click's coordinates default to (0,0). `applyLabelTier` (line 1578) sorts labels by priority (a place beats any landmark, which beats a quiet label) and lets only the first claimant of each `COLLISION_CELL_PX` (72px) grid cell survive. `ArrowLayer` (line 2399) draws each narrative leg as a paired casing+colored bezier `<path>`, boosted curvature for crowded clusters (`clusterKey`) so overlapping legs stay hoverable. `BorderLayer` (line 3112) owns two `<svg>` elements -- `_svg` (band/line/hit-strokes) and its own `_washSvg` in a dedicated pane so `mix-blend-mode: multiply` genuinely reaches the tile imagery (a documented fix, BLOCKER B1: a blend mode inside a stacking-context pane can only blend against siblings in that SAME pane) -- plus a land-mask clipPath and parallel settled/morph sub-groups toggled by `beginMorph`/`requestMorphFrame`/`settleMorph`. `_evaluateMorphFrame` (line 3617) is the CPU evaluator (calling border-morph.js's `lookup`+`animate` once per `requestAnimationFrame`); a documented, unbuilt GPU/WebGL swap seam is noted but not needed at this app's scale. `attachZoomAnim`/`resetZoomAnimTransform` (lines 2360, 2376) hand-roll Leaflet's own `L.Renderer` zoomanim recipe, since ArrowLayer/BorderLayer manage bare `<svg>` elements rather than `L.SVG`. Disclosed gaps: hover arbitration is best-effort, not a per-target geometric guarantee; a topology-changing morph (differing ring counts) snaps rather than interpolating. Depends on border-morph.js; used via JS interop by client/MapInterop.cs, and read directly by most of tests/ux/world-*.spec.ts and split-view.spec.ts.

files.l1: This document is the rulebook the whole test suite plays by: it lists every element name ("testid") a test is allowed to look for, every URL shape the app supports, and how years, ranges, and references are supposed to look on screen. A test is never allowed to know how a component is built internally -- only what this document promises exists. If the app changes how something renders, this document changes first (or alongside it), and every test still passes because it only ever asked for what's written here.

files.role: Playwright project config: base URL, timeouts, and the two webServer boot commands.
files.l1: This is the setup file that tells Playwright how to start the app before running tests, how long to wait for slow tests, and where the app lives (localhost:5000/8000). Without it, `npx playwright test` wouldn't know to launch the Rust API and the Blazor client first, or how long a genuinely slow property test is allowed to run before being called a failure.
files.l2: A single `defineConfig` call sets `timeout: 240_000` (240s per test -- raised twice, with the reasoning for each raise documented inline: once for the dense per-arrow assertion loop in api-scene.spec.ts, once for world-map.spec.ts's own linearly-slower-at-higher-FC_NUM_RUNS full page-reload property), `retries: 0`, and `use: { baseURL: 'http://localhost:5000' }`. The `webServer` array boots two processes before any test runs: `start-api.ps1` (the Rust server, `cargo run --release`, 300s boot budget for a cold release build) and `start-client.ps1` (the Blazor client, 180s budget), both with `reuseExistingServer: true` so a developer's own already-running dev servers are reused rather than restarted.
files.l3: The comment block above `timeout: 240_000` is itself a small incident report: it documents a real investigation where a property test's cost was mistakenly attributed to worker contention before being root-caused to Playwright's `expect()` call overhead at high call-volume (thousands of calls per iteration) -- the actual fix (api-scene.spec.ts's own plain `ok()` throw-helper) lives in that spec file, not here; this file's own 240s just gives real, still-slower-than-average tests (world-map.spec.ts's WORLD-1, a full `page.goto` reload per fast-check iteration) honest margin. `webServer`'s `url` health-check endpoints (`/health` for the API, the bare root for the client) are what Playwright polls before considering each server "ready".

files.role: Shared testid regex/selector excluding cluster glyphs from lit-marker counts.
files.l1: Once the map can collapse a crowd of markers into one numbered cluster glyph, a plain "count every marker-* element" check would wrongly include those cluster glyphs alongside real place markers. This file is the one shared pattern that correctly excludes them, so every existing "how many lit places are on screen" test keeps meaning what it always meant.
files.l2: Two exported constants: `LIT_MARKER_TESTID`, a regex `/^marker-(?!cluster-)/` for use with Playwright locators/JS matching, and `VISIBLE_LIT_MARKER_SELECTOR`, the equivalent as a raw CSS attribute selector with Playwright's `:visible` pseudo-class appended, for a caller that wants one specific visible marker (e.g. `.first()`) rather than a count.
files.l3: Both exist because map.js's cluster glyphs (`marker-cluster-{n}`) are deliberately namespaced under the same `marker-` prefix as every other marker kind (CONTRACT.md's own note); a bare `/^marker-/` locator predates clustering and would silently start matching cluster glyphs too. A `marker-{placeId}` element stays attached to the DOM (just hidden) even while absorbed into a cluster, so `VISIBLE_LIT_MARKER_SELECTOR`'s `:visible` filter is what's needed on top of the prefix exclusion for a caller that specifically wants an on-screen candidate.

files.role: Filters a candidate id list down to those whose marker/label is safely, unambiguously hoverable right now.
files.l1: The map can pack markers close enough together that even a real, forced test hover risks landing on the wrong one, or on a label that's currently hidden by anti-clutter rules. This file answers, for the CURRENTLY rendered page, "which of these candidate places can I safely hover and trust the result" -- so tests never depend on luck.
files.l2: `independentlyHoverableIds(page, ids)` measures every candidate's real on-screen marker center (`markerCenters`), plus every quiet-dot/cluster-glyph center currently on screen (`otherCandidateCenters`), and keeps only the ids whose center is at least `SAFE_NEIGHBOR_PX` (26px, matching map.js's own hit-circle diameter) away from every OTHER candidate AND every other on-screen marker kind, AND whose label survived collision damping (`labelIsVisible`). files.role: Proves VerseLine.BijectiveBase26's boundary values for the cross-reference superscript lettering scheme (a, b, ..., z, aa, ab, ...).
files.l1: A verse's cross-reference superscript letter is assigned by counting position among a chapter's xref-bearing verses, using the same letter scheme spreadsheet columns use -- so the 27th verse gets "aa", never wrapping back to "a". This file pins the exact boundary values where a naive modulo-26 scheme would have gotten it wrong.
files.l2: A [Theory] (or explicit [Fact]s) checking VerseLine.BijectiveBase26 at the six named boundary values: 26->"z", 27->"aa" (the exact collision point a fix-round-1 modulo bug got wrong), 52->"az", 53->"ba", 702->"zz", 703->"aaa".
files.l3: This directly documents and pins a real regression: an earlier version used plain `ordinal % 26`, which collided the 27th verse's letter back onto "a" -- bijective base-26 numeration (no digit for zero) never collides.

files.role: Proves state-atom laws 4 (confluence) and 5 (agreement): the final value never depends on subscriber count or dispatch interleaving, and every live projection agrees after every dispatch.
files.l1: The app's shared state atoms have to behave the same regardless of how many components happen to be listening, or the exact order two callers' updates land in. This file proves that with generated, seeded (never wall-clock-random) sequences of intents over a real StateAtom, using a throwaway synthetic Counter type rather than any real feature's state.
files.l2: Uses hand-rolled, seeded System.Random generators (Generators.cs) to build reproducible intent sequences over the real StateAtom<Counter>/Projection<Counter>, checking the final value matches a pure fold over the same sequence regardless of subscriber count, interleaving order, or re-entrant dispatch from inside a Changed handler.
files.l3: Law4_Confluence_FinalValueIsIndependentOfSubscriberCount and _FinalValueMatchesAPureFoldOverTheSameSequence are the core confluence proofs; _ReEntrantDispatchFromInsideAChangedHandlerIsHandledConsistently covers a trickier re-entrancy edge case; Law5_Agreement_AllProjectionsAgreeAfterEveryDispatch is the agreement law.

files.role: The largest single conformance file: a battery of repo-wide scans proving the state-atom migration's own architectural rules hold everywhere, not just where a developer remembered to apply them.
files.l1: This file doesn't test one feature's behavior -- it reads through the real client/ source tree and enforces several structural rules at once: effects only ever subscribe via the registry (never a raw .Changed += outside an allowlist), no component holds its own copy of migrated atom state, and atom/effect names are all registered as real, singleton, uniquely-named services. Every rule is proven to have real teeth via a matching, deliberately-broken planted example.
files.l2: Follows the established conformance-scan discipline this project uses repeatedly (AsyncMemoConformanceTests.cs, PopoverChromeConformanceTests.cs): a RepoRoot file scan, a comment-stripped source read, a bounded regex per rule, and a shared predicate exercised by both the real scan and a planted violation. AtomRegistrationConformance additionally resolves a REAL IServiceCollection/ServiceProvider (via AppServices, the same code Program.cs calls) to prove singleton lifetime, not just construction.
files.l3: Key groups of tests: EffectsOnlyViaRegistry_* (an allowlist keyed on subscription expression text, not a fragile line number); AtomRegistrationConformance_* (singleton lifetime + unique names); NoComponentHeldSharedState_*/NoComponentHeldArrangementState_*/NoComponentHeldOtherAtomState_* (each with several Planted*_IsCaught self-checks plus a NoRealSite... sweep); RoleFormulaRederivation_*; ViewIdentityVsCapability_*; and a documented, disclosed limitation (StripLineComments_DisclosedLimitation_ASlashSlashInsideAStringLiteralSilentlyEatsTheRestOfTheLine) in its own comment-stripping helper.

files.role: Proves EffectRegistry's five semantic guarantees: one owner per effect name, latest-claim-wins, release-on-dispose, reconcile-on-claim, and AppliesTo gating.
files.l1: Effects are the mechanism that reacts to a state atom changing (e.g. saving to localStorage). This file makes sure only ONE effect can own a given name at a time, that claiming a name again supersedes the old owner cleanly, that disposing releases it, and that a freshly-claimed effect fires once immediately even if the value hasn't changed since the last claim.
files.l2: Uses the same synthetic Counter/SetCounter vocabulary as StateAtomLawTests.cs (Generators.cs) over a small, purpose-built DelegateEffect<T>, requiring no new production types beyond what the state-atom layer already ships.
files.l3: LatestClaimWins_* and ReleaseOnDispose_* cover ownership transfer and cleanup; ReconcileOnClaim_* covers the claim-time "materialize once even if unchanged" guarantee; AppliesToGating_* covers conditional effects; TwoRapidReClaims_* includes both a positive case and a documented NEGATIVE control (DispatchWhileThePriorClaimIsStillHeldDoubleMaterializes) proving the guarantee only holds when dispose happens first.

files.role: Proves the popover-back-stack ownership hand-off mechanism (which of several live popover instances gets to reclaim the shared atom when the active one closes), without a live Blazor host.
files.l1: If more than one popover session could exist at once (a controller ruling required this be tested), closing the currently-active one has to correctly hand control to another still-live one, if any -- never to two at once, and never leaving a dangling reference if none remain.
files.l2: A FakePopover class independently re-implements ExplorerPopover.razor's own ApplyLocally/OnFocusStackChanged logic (documented per method) against the REAL FocusStack/OwnershipRegistry/StateAtom types -- not a mock, a second real implementation of the same algorithm, so a bug in either copy is likely to surface as a mismatch rather than agreeing with itself.
files.l3: AdjudicationE_ClosingTheActiveSessionLetsAnotherLiveSupersededPopoverReclaimAndReseed is the primary hand-off proof; _WithNoOtherLiveInstanceLeavesTheAtomReset and _WithThreeLiveInstances_OnlyOneReclaims_TheOthersStayInert cover the boundary cases.

files.role: Proves the FocusStack atom's own Visit/Back/Reset/SeedFromTrail behavior and law coverage, over a real VerseNode.
files.l1: This is the state atom behind the popover's own "back" button and its saved-exploration trail -- this file checks visiting a new node pushes and records the trail, going back pops correctly and records the landing (without double-recording a consecutive repeat), and seeding from a saved trail restores it in order.

files.role: Hand-rolled, seeded, deterministic pseudo-random sequence generators for the synthetic Counter/SetCounter state-law test vocabulary.
files.l1: The five state-law tests need many different, reproducible sequences of "pretend user actions" to replay against the state-atom infrastructure. This file is what generates those sequences -- always the same sequence for the same seed, on any machine, with no new external dependency.
files.l2: Provides seeded System.Random-based generator helpers producing sequences of the throwaway Counter/SetCounter/ResetCounter intents used across StateAtomLawTests.cs, ConfluenceAgreementLawTests.cs, NoEchoLawTests.cs, and EffectRegistryTests.cs.
files.l3: The file's own header states the house law explicitly: "never wall-clock random; no new test dependency without disclosure -- prefer none" -- satisfied here by System.Random(int seed), which .NET documents as a stable, deterministic PRNG, not wall-clock based, so a fixed checked-in seed reproduces identically across runs and machines.

files.role: Proves state-atom law 3 (no-echo): a genuinely oscillation-prone bidirectional link pair settles after exactly one hop, never cascading forever.
files.l1: If two pieces of shared state are linked in both directions (each one's change updates the other), a naive implementation could bounce back and forth forever. This file builds a deliberately oscillation-prone pair (where neither side's derive function is a fixed point of the other) and proves the real link-runner mechanism stops the cascade after exactly one hop.
files.l2: Wires two synthetic Counter atoms together via StateLinkRunner<A,B> in both directions live, dispatches a change into one side, and counts exactly how many hops the update propagates before settling.
files.l3: This is described as "the meatiest of the five [state] laws" in its own header comment; Law3_NoEcho_ABidirectionalPairSettlesAfterExactlyOneHop_OverAGeneratedSequence is the core proof, Law3_NoEcho_ALinkThatIsInactiveNeverParticipatesInTheEcho is the companion guard for a deactivated link.

files.role: Proves the Selection atom's Toggle/Remove/Clear behavior and its idempotent-toggle-PAIRS property (two toggles of the same item return to the original list).
files.l1: This is the state behind the multi-select Selection Tray -- toggling an item twice should leave the list exactly as it started, but a SINGLE toggle is deliberately NOT idempotent (redispatching it twice flips it twice, proven as an explicit negative control).
files.l2: Uses SequenceEqualityComparer<T> (proven correct in its own two tests first, since the default comparer would wrongly treat two distinct-but-same-content list instances as unequal) to compare the ordered IReadOnlyList<ExplorationDescriptor> Selection value.
files.l3: IdempotentTogglePairs_HoldsOverAGeneratedSequenceOfPairedToggles is the generated-sequence law proof; NegativeControl_ToggleIsNotIndividuallyIdempotent_RedispatchingTheSameInstanceTwiceFlipsTwice is the deliberate negative control; Toggle_IdentityIsKindAndKey_NeverTitle pins that a title change alone never affects toggle identity.

files.role: Proves state-atom laws 1 (single-writer) and 2 (idempotence): a StateAtom's Value can only change via Dispatch, and redispatching the same intent instance is a no-op.
files.l1: This is the foundational contract every shared piece of app state relies on: nothing can mutate an atom's value except its own Dispatch method, and dispatching the exact same instruction twice in a row should never fire a second change notification.
files.l2: Uses the synthetic Counter/SetCounter/ResetCounter vocabulary (Generators.cs) over a real StateAtom<Counter>, deliberately outliving any one specific migration (Locus, TimeWindow, or whatever a later batch adds).
files.l3: Law1_SingleWriter_ValuePropertyHasNoPublicSetter and _DispatchIsTheOnlyPublicWayToChangeValue pin the write-access rule via reflection/compile-time shape; Law2_Idempotence_ADeltaIntentIsCorrectlyNOTIdempotent_NegativeControl is the deliberate negative control proving a genuinely-different (delta) intent is correctly NOT idempotent.

files.role: Proves StateLinkRunner<A,B>'s imperative mechanics: it only derives while Active, SyncNow forces a derivation without a source change, and Dispose unsubscribes cleanly.
files.l1: This is the non-law, plumbing-level half of the bidirectional-link mechanism NoEchoLawTests.cs proves the no-echo LAW for -- this file just checks the runner wires up, activates/deactivates, and tears down correctly.
files.l2: Constructs a DelegateLink<Counter,Counter> between two real StateAtoms and a StateLinkRunner over it, asserting derivation only happens while Active, that SyncNow works even with no source change, and that both constructor-arg-mismatch cases throw.
files.l3: WhileActive_SourceChangeDispatchesTheDerivedValueIntoTarget_TaggedWithTheGivenName and WhileInactive_SourceChangeNeverTouchesTarget are the core activation gate; Dispose_UnsubscribesFromSourceChanged_NoFurtherDerivation proves cleanup.

files.role: THE COUNTING LAW made real: proves the number of Reqnroll scenarios this assembly actually discovered equals the number declared in the committed .feature files.
files.l1: The controller's own ruling requires that the client-side and Rust-side contract-test counts must always match exactly -- any divergence means a feature file is being run on one side but not the other. This file is that check, made real: it reflects over the compiled test assembly to count discovered scenarios, and separately parses the raw .feature text files to count declared ones, then asserts they're equal.
files.l2: CountDiscoveredReqnrollScenarios uses System.Reflection to count every SkippableFactAttribute (one plain scenario) plus every InlineDataAttribute (one Scenario Outline row) across the assembly's generated code-behind; CountScenariosInFeatureFiles independently, textually (language-agnostic, no Reqnroll/cucumber-specific parsing) counts "Scenario:" lines and Examples-table data rows in the real .feature files under contracts/atlas-query-contract/features/.
files.l3: DiscoveredScenarioCountMatchesTheCommittedFeatureFiles is the single assertion; it exists specifically to catch a feature file silently failing to link into the project (a stale ReqnrollFeatureFile glob, a build-config gap) that would let the discovered count quietly fall behind the declared one.

files.role: The Reqnroll step-definition glue binding every phrase in the atlas-query-contract's Gherkin feature files to the client's own DTO deserialization against committed fixtures, never a live server.
files.l1: This file is the translator between plain-English Gherkin sentences ("Given a FocusQuery request for...") and real C# code that runs the client's own JSON deserialization against a pre-recorded server response. It's deliberately thin -- it knows how to bind phrases, not what the contract itself means -- so the SAME feature files can be proven correct against both the C# client and, separately, a Rust cucumber harness.
files.l2: One Reqnroll [Binding] class, instantiated fresh per scenario (mirroring the Rust harness's own AqcWorld). Loads contracts/atlas-query-contract/aqc.schema.json once (replacing an old hand-copied required-field switch that three places used to carry independently) and a wire-id-to-fixture-name identity index (contracts/atlas-query-contract/fixtures/index.json, built by the Rust exporter) so a captured reference is checked against a genuinely independent, generated table rather than the same deterministic function called twice.
files.l3: Instance fields (_status, _body, _capturedRef) are this scenario's own "World" state. The IdentityIndex/ErrorCaseFixtures split matters: a captured FocusQuery reference that isn't a real key in the generated index throws immediately, which is what makes WhenFocusQueryCaptured's second lookup a genuinely independently-failable check rather than a vacuous self-comparison -- a documented fix-round finding (S-1).
